query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys, multi‐element segregation concentrated at the grain boundaries governs structural and chemical stability at high temperature by suppressing grain boundary migration and interfacial chemical diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline or ultrafine-grained high-entropy nanoalloys with a uniform bulk composition and unmodified grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Engineering the alloy composition to promote multi-element grain boundary decoration via controlled segregation during processing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (e.g., 600–1000 °C) under which diffusional kinetics are activated, mimicking operational or thermal cycling environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries enriched with multiple elements (a high configurational entropy interfacial phase) that reduce boundary energy and mobility.
generation.mechanism: The retained multi-element decoration increases local configurational entropy and lowers the driving force for boundary migration and chemical diffusion, effectively retarding grain coarsening and phase degradation under high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoalloys with engineered multi-element segregated grain boundaries will exhibit slower grain growth, more stable phase distributions, and improved retention of nanostructural and chemical homogeneity, compared to alloys lacking such controlled segregation.
generation.baseline: High-entropy nanoalloys processed without targeted grain boundary segregation, which are expected to show faster grain growth and more pronounced chemical inhomogeneity upon long-term high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold under temperatures where diffusion is significant but below thresholds (>1050 °C) where extensive atomic interdiffusion or phase transformations occur; extreme mechanical loading conditions might also alter the stabilization mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative effects on grain boundary mobility and the exact temperature range for effective stabilization remain uncertain and require systematic calibration; additional factors such as alloy-specific thermodynamics may influence results.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy samples: one with engineered multi-element grain boundary segregation and a control set without targeted segregation. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature dwell cycles and monitor microstructural evolution.
measurements: Grain boundary chemical composition using atom probe tomography
Retention of mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in grain growth rates and enhanced phase or chemical stability relative to the control samples under high-temperature conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). Theoretical Prediction of Strengthening in Nanocrystalline Cu with Multi-Element Grain Boundary Segregation Decoration

Abstract: AbstractThe composition of grain boundaries (GBs) determines their mechanical behavior, which in turn affects the mechanical properties of nanocrystalline materials. Inspired by GB segregation and the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), we investigated, respectively, the mechanical responses of nanocrystalline Cu samples with and without multi-element GBs, as well as the grain size effects, aiming to explore the effects of GB composition decoration on mechanical properties. Our results show that introducing multi-element segregation GBs can significantly improve the mechanical properties of nanocrystalline Cu by effectively inhibiting GB migration and sliding. Additionally, we proposed an improved a theoretical model that can reasonably describe the strengths of the materials with multi-element or single-element segregation GBs. Notably, the introduction of multi-element segregation GBs inhibits both migration and sliding behavior, with migration being more effectively suppressed than sliding.
